subtasks.summary: Lets one job be broken into smaller jobs underneath it. The parent stays the thing you scheduled and reported on; the children are the pieces somebody actually ticks off during the day.
subtasks.caption: One parent job, with its own smaller jobs beneath it.
steps: Open a job and add the smaller pieces of work it really consists of.
Each subtask can be assigned to a different person and finished separately.
The parent shows how much of it is done, so progress is visible without opening it.
benefits: A long job stops looking like a single unmoving card on the board
Two people can work different parts of the same job at once
Progress you can see at a glance instead of asking

fit.on: A single job routinely takes more than a day, or more than one person.
fit.off: Work arrives already small — one visit, one fix, one person.

subtasks.caveat: Subtasks are pieces of their parent, not jobs in their own right: they do not appear as separate work on the board or in reports.

checklists.summary: A tick-list inside a job. Use it for the steps that must happen every time and must be seen to have happened — a safety check, a handover, the things an inspector will ask about later.
checklists.caption: Items ticked off in order, with the last one still open.
steps: Add the items to the job, or to the task type so every job of that kind starts with them.
Whoever does the work ticks each item as they go, on the phone or on the web.
The record of what was ticked, and when, stays on the job.
benefits: The same standard applied on every visit, by everyone
Evidence that a step was completed, not just claimed
New people can do unfamiliar work without being talked through it

fit.on: Consistency matters, or somebody may later ask you to prove a step was done.
fit.off: The work varies so much that a fixed list would only be noise.

checklists.caveat: A checklist records that an item was ticked — it does not stop a job being finished with items outstanding. Use a workflow if you need it to be enforced.

attachments.summary: Photos and documents attached to a job. Uploaded straight from the phone on site, kept with the job rather than in somebody's camera roll or a message thread.
attachments.caption: Files kept with the job they belong to.
steps: Attach from the phone camera, the gallery, or from a file on the web.
Everyone with access to the job sees the same files, immediately.
Files stay attached to the job for as long as the job is kept.
benefits: Before-and-after evidence in the place it belongs
No hunting through chats for the photo somebody took
The same file for the office and the person on site

fit.on: The work produces anything visual, or you need proof of condition.
fit.off: Nobody photographs anything and no paperwork changes hands.

attachments.caveat: Attachments count towards your storage, and large videos consume it quickly. Photos are compressed before upload; other files are stored as they are.

dependencies.summary: Says that one job cannot start until another has finished. The board and the schedule then reflect the real order of work rather than a list of things that all look equally ready.
dependencies.caption: Work that must happen in order — the last step only opens once the earlier ones close.
steps: Link a job to the one it waits on.
A job whose predecessor is unfinished is shown as blocked rather than available.
When the earlier job closes, the next one opens on its own.
benefits: Nobody starts work that cannot actually be started yet
The knock-on effect of a delay is visible immediately
Sequenced work can be planned without a spreadsheet beside it

fit.on: Jobs genuinely wait on each other — a fit-out, an install, a staged repair.
fit.off: Every job stands alone and can be done in any order.

dependencies.caveat: Dependencies describe order, not dates. A blocked job does not move itself in the calendar when the job it waits on slips.

custom_fields.summary: Extra fields on a job, defined by you. Meter readings, serial numbers, a reference from the client's own system — whatever this kind of work needs recorded in a consistent place.
custom_fields.caption: Your own fields, filled in as part of the job.
steps: Define the fields on a task type, so every job of that kind asks for them.
The fields appear on the job for whoever does the work to fill in.
What was entered can be read back in reports and exports.
benefits: Information captured the same way every time, not in free text
Values you can actually report on afterwards
Different kinds of work can ask for different things

fit.on: You keep asking people to write the same detail into the description.
fit.off: The description and a photo already cover everything.

custom_fields.caveat: Fields belong to a task type. Moving a job to a different type drops the fields the new type does not ask for — the values are not carried across.

tracking.summary: Records the route taken to a job while somebody is on their way, and shows where people on the road are now. It is about the journey to the work, not about watching people all day.
tracking.caption: The actual path taken between two stops.
steps: Recording starts when the person marks themselves on the way, and stops when they arrive.
The live map shows who is where, so the next job goes to whoever is nearest.
The finished route stays on the job, with distance and time.
benefits: Distance and travel time you can bill or reimburse without a claim form
An answer to "how long until someone gets here" that is not a guess
A record of the journey if a visit is ever disputed

fit.on: People drive between jobs and the travel is part of the cost.
fit.off: Everyone works at one site, or travel is not yours to account for.

tracking.caveat: Recording only runs between setting off and arriving — never for the rest of the day. It needs background location permission on the phone, and the person is told when it is on.

service_reports.summary: The record of what was done, produced at the end of a job: the work carried out, parts used, photos, and signatures from both your engineer and the customer.
service_reports.caption: One report per job, filed with everything it needs.
steps: The person finishing the job fills in what was done and any parts used.
Both sides sign on the phone — your engineer, and whoever is there for the customer.
The finished report stays on the job and on the asset's history.
benefits: Proof of work signed on site, not chased afterwards
Parts recorded where the cost can be seen against the job
A maintenance history that builds itself as jobs are completed

fit.on: Customers expect a record of the visit, or you invoice for work done.
fit.off: The job is finished when it is marked finished and nobody asks for more.

service_reports.caveat: A report can be corrected for a short window after completion; after that it is fixed, because its value is that it was signed at the time.

assets.summary: The things you look after — machines, vehicles, apartments, equipment — kept as records with their own history, so a job can be about a specific item and not just an address.
assets.caption: One record per thing, with its history filed underneath.
steps: Define the kinds of asset you look after and what each kind needs recorded.
Attach a job to an asset instead of only to a place.
Every completed job adds to that asset's history automatically.
benefits: The full service history of an item in one place
Recurring maintenance that follows the item, not a calendar note
An answer to "when was this last touched, and by whom"

fit.on: You service the same items repeatedly, or manage property.
fit.off: Every job is a one-off at a different place.

assets.caveat: An asset belongs to its kind, and the kind belongs to a workspace. Moving an asset between workspaces means changing its kind, and fields the new kind does not ask for are dropped.

time_tracking.summary: Turns a workspace into somewhere people clock in and out. It records what actually happened, and separately works out what should be paid — so a shift that started early or ran late does not become an argument at the end of the month.
time_tracking.caption: Arriving early is recorded, and paid from the shift start. The same applies at the end.
steps: People clock in from the phone or the web. If the workspace has an address, the app checks they are there; a workspace with no coordinates skips that check.
Rests are planned for the workspace, prompted at the right time, and recorded as taken or missed.
Finishing short, or running past the shift, raises a request that goes to whoever is responsible for that person.
Only flagged shifts need review — clean ones approve themselves.
benefits: Hours per person and workspace, ready for payroll
An approval trail showing who accepted which hours
Late starts, early finishes and missed rests surfaced as they happen
People working away from any site can clock in too, where you allow it

fit.on: People are paid for time rather than for a finished job.
fit.off: You care that the work is done, not when somebody arrived.

time_tracking.caveat: Working away from a site needs two things: the workspace must allow it and the person must be granted it. Neither alone is enough, so a strict site cannot be opened up by one person's settings.

sprints.summary: Fixed periods of work that a set of jobs is committed to. Useful when a team plans in weeks rather than reacting to whatever arrives.
sprints.caption: A period of work, with what was committed and what actually landed.
steps: Open a sprint for the period you plan in.
Move the jobs you intend to finish into it.
At the end, see what completed and what carried over.
benefits: A team that knows what this period is for
A visible difference between planned and actual
A basis for judging how much fits in the next one

fit.on: Work is planned in cycles by a team that decides its own load.
fit.off: Jobs arrive from customers and are done in the order they arrive.

sprints.caveat: Sprints suit planned work. If your day is driven by incoming calls, a sprint mostly measures how often the plan was interrupted.

story_points.summary: A size on each job, so a team can talk about how much work something is without pretending to know how many hours it takes.
story_points.caption: Sizes rolled up, so a period's load can be compared to the last one.
steps: Put a size on jobs when planning, using whatever scale the team agrees.
Sizes add up across a sprint or a period.
Compare periods to see what the team actually gets through.
benefits: A shared sense of size that survives an optimistic estimate
Load compared between periods rather than guessed
A planning conversation that is not about hours

fit.on: A team plans together and wants to size work honestly.
fit.off: Jobs are broadly similar, or you already track hours.

story_points.caveat: Points only mean something within one team. Comparing them between teams, or turning them into hours, gives the number an authority it does not have.

epics.summary: A larger piece of work that many jobs belong to — a project, a site, a campaign. The jobs stay separate; the epic is how you see them as one thing.
epics.caption: Many jobs, gathered under the larger thing they serve.
steps: Create the epic for the larger goal.
Attach jobs to it as they are created or afterwards.
The epic shows how much of the whole is finished.
benefits: Progress on a project without counting cards by hand
Jobs that keep their own owners and dates
A way to report on a project rather than on tasks

fit.on: Work naturally clusters into projects that run for weeks or months.
fit.off: Every job is independent and finished within days.

epics.caveat: An epic groups work; it does not schedule it. Closing an epic does not close the jobs inside it.

phases.summary: The stages a piece of work passes through — survey, quote, install, sign-off. Where a workflow governs one job, phases describe the shape of a whole project.
phases.caption: The stages of a project, one following the other.
steps: Define the phases this kind of project goes through.
Put each job into the phase it belongs to.
See what is outstanding in each phase rather than one long list.
benefits: A project read as stages instead of a flat backlog
A clear view of where work is piling up
Reporting by stage, for clients who ask in those terms

fit.on: Projects run long enough to have distinct stages.
fit.off: Work is short and moves straight from booked to done.

phases.caveat: Phases group jobs within a project. They are not statuses — a job still moves through its own workflow inside whichever phase it sits in.

crm.summary: The record of who you work for. Companies, the people at them, what was agreed and what has been done — kept beside the work instead of in a separate address book.
crm.caption: Your side and the client's, kept against one shared record.
steps: Add the companies you work for, and the people you deal with at each.
Jobs, quotes and history attach to the client record.
Anyone with access sees the same account, not their own copy.
benefits: One place to look before a call, instead of three
History that survives whoever used to handle the account
Contacts kept as people, so one person can work at several firms

fit.on: You work for repeat clients rather than one-off callers.
fit.off: Work comes through one channel and the client rarely matters afterwards.

crm.caveat: A contact person is not a client: contacts are not counted as clients and are not billed as such, so a firm with six contacts is still one client.

b2c_portal.summary: Gives your clients a login of their own, where they can raise a request and follow it, without phoning or emailing anyone.
b2c_portal.caption: The client's side and yours, meeting at the same request.
steps: Set up the portal for the workspace and decide what clients may raise.
Invite clients; they get a login limited strictly to their own requests.
Requests arrive as work on your board, already attributed.
benefits: Requests that arrive complete instead of as a phone message
Clients who can see progress without asking
Fewer calls asking whether something was received

fit.on: Clients raise work themselves and expect to see where it stands.
fit.off: Work arrives from one contact who prefers to call.

b2c_portal.caveat: Portal users see strictly their own requests and nothing else. The portal needs the CRM module, because a request has to belong to a client.

space_sharing.summary: Lets another organization work inside one of your workspaces — a subcontractor, a partner, a client's own team — with exactly the access you grant and no more.
space_sharing.caption: Two organizations, one shared workspace between them.
steps: Share the workspace with the other organization and choose what they may do.
Their people see that workspace, and nothing else of yours.
Stop sharing and the access ends, while the history stays.
benefits: Subcontractors working in your system instead of over email
Access that ends cleanly when the relationship does
One version of the work, not two that drift apart

fit.on: Other companies do work that has to land in your system.
fit.off: All the work is done by your own people.

space_sharing.caveat: Sharing is per workspace and is re-checked continuously — removing a share takes effect immediately, and the other side keeps no copy.

workflows.summary: Lets you replace the built-in job statuses with your own, and decide which status may follow which. A boiler service and a building inspection do not move through the same stages, and this is where you say so.
workflows.caption: Only the moves you allow are possible — a job cannot skip to the end.
steps: Build a workflow, or start from a template and edit it.
Assign it to a task type, so different work can follow different routes.
The board, the allowed moves and the phone's buttons all follow what you defined.
benefits: Statuses in your words rather than the software's
Impossible transitions blocked, so the board reflects reality
A different route per kind of work, across every workspace

fit.on: Your process has stages the standard statuses do not describe.
fit.off: The built-in statuses already match how you work.

workflows.caveat: Choosing an existing workflow is always free — building your own is what this buys. It is bought once for the organization and applies everywhere.

recurring.summary: Jobs that create themselves on a schedule — a monthly service, a weekly inspection — so the work appears when it is due instead of when somebody remembers.
recurring.caption: The same job, arriving again each time it is due.
steps: Set the pattern on a job: how often, and in which workspace.
Each occurrence is created as a real job when it comes due.
Change the pattern and future occurrences follow; past ones stay as they were.
benefits: Planned maintenance that does not depend on memory
A forward view of committed work
Occurrences that can be reassigned or edited individually

fit.on: Some of your work happens on a cycle you have promised to keep.
fit.off: Everything is reactive and scheduled when it is asked for.

recurring.caveat: An occurrence becomes an ordinary job the moment it is created. Editing the pattern afterwards does not rewrite occurrences that already exist.

shift_scheduling.summary: Plan who works when, publish it, and let the clock compare what happened against what was planned. Without a rota, time tracking still records hours — it just has nothing to measure them against.
shift_scheduling.caption: The plan, and what actually happened against it.
steps: Build the rota for the workspace and publish it to the team.
People see their own shifts on the phone.
Clocking in and out is compared with the shift, and differences are flagged.
benefits: A rota people can see without being sent a picture of one
Late starts, early finishes and no-shows surfaced automatically
The planned hours that make paid hours meaningful

fit.on: People work set hours you decide in advance.
fit.off: People work when the jobs require it, with no fixed pattern.

shift_scheduling.caveat: This is what gives time tracking its planned shift. On its own it plans; paired with time tracking it also flags what did not go to plan.

overtime.summary: The approval path for time beyond the planned shift. Extra time is requested, goes to whoever is responsible for that person, and is either approved or not — with a signature.
overtime.caption: A request, a decision, and a record of both.
steps: Somebody works past their shift, or finishes short, and a request is raised.
It goes to the person responsible for them, with the hours and a signature.
Approving moves the paid hours; refusing leaves them as planned.
benefits: Extra hours agreed rather than discovered on a payslip
A record of who approved what, and when
Payroll figures nobody has to reconstruct afterwards

fit.on: Extra time happens and somebody has to agree to pay for it.
fit.off: Hours are fixed, or extra time is handled outside the system.

overtime.caveat: Approving extra time moves the end of the shift, which is what makes it paid — there is no separate overtime rate here, only agreed hours.

invoicing.summary: Turn completed work into invoices for your clients, using what the jobs already recorded — hours, parts, and what was agreed.
invoicing.caption: Work and costs rolled up into what a client owes.
steps: Completed jobs carry their hours, parts and any agreed rate.
Build an invoice for a client from the work in a period.
Send it, and track what has been paid.
benefits: Invoices built from the work rather than retyped from it
Less time between finishing a job and billing it
Fewer arguments, because the detail is already recorded

fit.on: You bill clients for work rather than being paid a salary.
fit.off: Billing happens in a finance system that already has what it needs.

invoicing.caveat: This invoices your clients. It is entirely separate from what you pay us — that is on the billing page and is not affected.

reports_builder.summary: Build your own reports from the data you already have: choose what to measure, how to group it, and over what period, without exporting anything.
reports_builder.caption: Figures gathered and rolled up into an answer.
steps: Pick what to measure and how to break it down.
Run it over the period you care about.
Save it, so the same question can be asked again next month.
benefits: Answers without a spreadsheet export
Questions saved once and re-asked whenever needed
The same numbers for everyone, rather than each person's own cut

fit.on: You regularly ask questions the standard screens do not answer.
fit.off: The dashboards already tell you what you need.

reports_builder.caveat: A report only sees data the reader is allowed to see, so the same report can show different totals to different people. That is deliberate.

report_scheduling.summary: Sends a saved report on a schedule, to the people who need it, without anyone remembering to run it.
report_scheduling.caption: The same report, arriving on its own each period.
steps: Save a report you want regularly.
Set when it should go, and to whom.
It arrives by email on that schedule.
benefits: Numbers that turn up without being chased
Everyone reading the same figures on the same day
One less recurring task in somebody's week

fit.on: Somebody currently runs the same report by hand every week or month.
fit.off: Reports are looked at when a question comes up, not on a cycle.

report_scheduling.caveat: Needs the report builder, since it sends saved reports. Recipients receive figures scoped to their own access, not the sender's.

audit_log.summary: A record of every change: who did it, what changed, and when. It is the answer to "who moved this" when nobody remembers.
audit_log.caption: Every change filed in order, oldest underneath.
steps: Changes are recorded as they happen, with no action needed from anyone.
Open the history on a job, a member or a workspace to see its trail.
The record cannot be edited, which is what makes it worth having.
benefits: An answer to who changed something, without asking around
Evidence for disputes about hours, status or access
A trail for auditors that does not have to be assembled

fit.on: You need to account for changes, or disputes come up.
fit.off: The team is small enough that asking is faster than looking.

audit_log.caveat: Entries are kept for a fixed retention period and then removed. It records changes made in the app — not conversations elsewhere.

documents.summary: The personnel file: what you issue to people, such as contracts and payslips, and what they supply to you, such as a passport or a licence. With signing, expiry and reminders.
documents.caption: One file per person, with everything issued and supplied.
steps: Define the kinds of document you handle, and who may see each kind.
Issue documents to people, or ask them to supply theirs.
Documents route for signature, and expiring ones are chased automatically.
benefits: A personnel file that is not a shared drive
Signatures collected in the app, with evidence of who signed
Expiring licences noticed before they expire

fit.on: You employ people and hold documents about them.
fit.off: Everyone is a contractor and paperwork lives elsewhere.

documents.caveat: Each document type names the roles that may see it, so the person chasing driving licences need not see payslips. A type with no roles named is visible to everyone who may view documents — that is the default, not a restriction.

priority_routing.summary: Puts your support requests at the front of the queue, with a response time we commit to rather than aim for.
priority_routing.caption: Requests sorted, with yours taken first.
steps: Raise support requests exactly as you do now.
Yours are picked up ahead of the standard queue.
Response times are committed, and measured.
benefits: A faster first response when something is wrong
A commitment rather than an expectation
Less waiting when the problem is stopping work

fit.on: Downtime costs you money and waiting is expensive.
fit.off: Questions can wait a day without anything going wrong.

priority_routing.caveat: This covers how quickly we respond, not how quickly every problem is solved — some need a fix that takes longer than a reply.

live_chat.summary: Talk to a person in the app, while you have the problem in front of you, instead of writing it up and waiting.
steps: Open chat from anywhere in the app.
Describe the problem while you are looking at it.
The conversation stays with your account for reference.
benefits: Answers in minutes rather than a round of emails
No writing up a problem you can simply show
A record of what was said, kept with your account

fit.on: Your team hits questions during the working day and cannot pause.
fit.off: Occasional questions that email handles perfectly well.

live_chat.caveat: Live chat is staffed during business hours. Outside them a message becomes a normal support request and is answered when the day starts.

dedicated_support.summary: A named person who knows your setup, rather than whoever picks up the ticket.
steps: You are introduced to the person who looks after your account.
They learn how you are set up, so you stop re-explaining it.
They handle your requests and escalate on your behalf.
benefits: Somebody who already knows your configuration
No re-explaining your setup with every request
A person to take a problem to, not a queue

fit.on: Your setup is large or unusual enough that context matters.
fit.off: The product does what you need and questions are rare.

dedicated_support.caveat: A named contact works business hours in their own timezone. Urgent matters outside those hours go through the normal support path.
